M. Manlius, consul in 392, was the hero of the defence of the Capitol in 390: woken by the cackling of Juno's sacred geese as Gauls climbed the cliff at night, he rushed to the edge, struck the first Gaul down, and rallied the defenders. He was rewarded with gifts of grain and wine from each soldier, and Roman tradition derived his cognomen Capitolinus from the exploit, though it probably came from the family's residence on the Capitol. His house stood on the Arx.

After the sack, jealous of Camillus' fame and moved, says Livy, by the misery of debtors, he became the plebs' champion. In 385 he paid from his own purse the debt of a decorated centurion being led away in bondage, sold his estate at Veii to free 400 debtors, and accused the patricians of hiding the gold intended for the Gallic ransom. The Senate appointed a dictator, A. Cornelius Cossus, who imprisoned him; the plebs' outcry forced his release. In 384 he was tried for aiming at kingship. In the Campus Martius, where he could point to the Capitol he had saved and display the spoils of 30 enemies, the people would not condemn him; the trial was moved to the Peteline grove, out of sight of the citadel, and he was condemned and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock, the place of his triumph. His house was razed, the site later given to the temple of Juno Moneta, and the Manlian gens resolved that no patrician Manlius would again bear the praenomen Marcus.

Manlius completes the trio of early 'tyrants' with Sp. Cassius and Sp. Maelius. Livy's account echoes the Catilinarian and Gracchan crises, but the debt problem of the 380s was real, and the political use of debt relief by an ambitious aristocrat is plausible. The paradox of the saviour of the Capitol thrown from it fascinated ancient writers.

T. Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus embodied the severity of the 4th-century Roman aristocracy. As a slow-spoken youth he was banished to the family's farm by his harsh father, L. Manlius Imperiosus; when a tribune prosecuted the father in 362 the son forced him at knifepoint to drop the case. Elected a military tribune, in 361 he answered the challenge of a huge Gaul at the bridge over the Anio and killed him, taking his torque (torques) and placing it, bloodstained, around his own neck; the soldiers' jesting cognomen Torquatus passed to his descendants. The annalist Claudius Quadrigarius' vivid description of the duel, quoted by Gellius, is one of the finest surviving passages of early Latin prose.

He was dictator in 353 against Caere, in 349 to hold elections and in 320, and consul in 347, 344 and 340. In the Latin War of 340, having ordered that no one should fight outside the ranks, he learned that his son had accepted a challenge from the Tusculan cavalry commander Geminus Maecius and killed him. He had his son bound to the stake and beheaded before the army; 'Manlian commands' (imperia Manliana) became proverbial, and the young men of Rome refused to go out to meet him when he returned in triumph. He led the Roman army at the battle of Vesuvius, where his colleague Decius devoted himself, and won again at Trifanum.

The Manlii Torquati kept his memory alive: a moneyer of the 60s BC put a torque border on his coins, and Cicero's friend L. Manlius Torquatus is the Epicurean spokesman in De finibus. The duel and the execution, whether or not exact, defined for later Romans the subordination of family to discipline.

M. Valerius Corvus (or Corvinus) had perhaps the longest career in Roman history. Pliny says he lived to 100 and that 46 years separated his first and sixth consulships. As a military tribune in 349 he accepted the challenge of a gigantic Gaul in the Pomptine territory; a raven landed on his helmet and attacked the Gaul's face with beak and claws, and Valerius killed him, taking the name Corvus. Augustus placed his statue among the great men in his Forum with a raven on its helmet.

He was elected consul at the age of 23 in 348, and again in 346, 343, 335, 300 and 299 (as suffect), dictator in 342 and 302 or 301, and held 21 curule offices in all. In 346 he defeated the Volsci and burned Satricum; in 343 he won the first great Roman victory over the Samnites at Mount Gaurus in Campania; in 342, as dictator, he calmed the mutiny of the Campanian garrison, granting amnesty and protection from arbitrary discharge; in 335 he took Cales, where a Latin colony followed; and as consul in 300 he carried the third lex Valeria on appeal, the first that most scholars accept as genuine, which made it a crime for a magistrate to scourge or execute a citizen who had appealed to the people. In 302 or 301 as dictator he campaigned against the Marsi and Etruscans and restored the Cilnii at Arretium.

Livy portrays him as an affable commander who shared the soldiers' games, the opposite of the stern Manlius. His career spans the critical half-century from the Gallic raids to the Third Samnite War, and its length, plausible in principle, may also have attracted episodes from homonymous Valerii.

C. Licinius Stolo was the plebeian tribune who, with L. Sextius Lateranus, led the decade-long campaign that ended in the laws of 367. Varro explains his cognomen: he was so careful a farmer that he dug out the useless suckers (stolones) from the roots of his trees and vines. Livy introduces him through his wife Fabia, younger daughter of the patrician M. Fabius Ambustus, whose envy of her sister, wife of a consular tribune, prompted her father to help his plebeian son-in-law win the consulship for men of his order.

Elected tribune from 376, Licinius and Sextius proposed three laws: relief of debt by deducting interest already paid, a ceiling of 500 iugera on holdings of public land, and the replacement of consular tribunes by consuls, one of whom must or might be plebeian. Re-elected year after year, they vetoed the election of curule magistrates and faced vetoes from colleagues won over by the patricians. They also carried the reform of the priestly board for the Sibylline Books, making it ten men, half plebeian. The laws passed in 367, and Sextius became the first plebeian consul in 366. Licinius was consul in 364 and 361, though the Fasti call the consul C. Licinius Calvus, and the identity of Stolo and Calvus is debated.

In 357 he was prosecuted by the plebeian aedile M. Popillius Laenas under his own law and fined 10,000 asses, because he and his emancipated son held 1,000 iugera of public land between them. The irony delighted ancient writers. Modern historians see Licinius as the leader of a wealthy plebeian elite seeking office, using the grievances of debtors and land-hungry farmers to build support, whose success created the patricio-plebeian nobility of the Middle Republic. The 500-iugera limit was revived, or invented in Livy's sources, by Ti. Gracchus in 133.

P. Decius Mus was a plebeian whose family became the type of self-sacrifice for the state. As a military tribune in 343, during the First Samnite War, he saved the army of the consul A. Cornelius Cossus, trapped in a valley near Saticula, by seizing a hill above the Samnites with a detachment, drawing their attack, and breaking out at night through their sleeping camp. The army awarded him the grass crown (corona graminea or obsidionalis), the highest Roman military decoration, given by soldiers to the man who saved them from a siege, together with a golden crown, 100 oxen and a white bull with gilded horns.

As consul in 340 with T. Manlius Torquatus he commanded against the Latins and Campanians. Both consuls dreamed that one side's general and the other side's army were owed to the Earth and the gods of the dead. At the battle near Vesuvius, when the Roman left under his command gave way, he called the pontifex M. Valerius, who dictated to him the formula of devotio, offering himself together with the enemy's army to the Di Manes and Tellus. Wearing the toga in the Gabine manner and standing on a spear, he recited the prayer, then rode into the enemy and was killed. His body was found the next day buried under enemy corpses, and his colleague gave him a splendid funeral.

Livy's text of the devotio is the most important document of the ritual, though its authenticity and that of the act itself are debated. His son devoted himself at Sentinum (295), and his grandson was said to have done so at Ausculum (279). Cicero repeatedly cites the three Decii as the supreme example of patriotic death, and the family's glory showed that plebeian virtus could match patrician nobility.

Q. Publilius Philo was the most important plebeian statesman of the generation after the Licinio-Sextian laws. As consul in 339 he defeated the Latins on the Fenectane plains and triumphed. Named dictator the same year, he carried three laws that Livy calls 'most favourable to the plebs and most damaging to the nobility': that plebiscites should bind all citizens; that the patrician senators should give their approval (auctoritas patrum) to laws proposed in the centuriate assembly in advance, before the vote, so that the patricians could no longer annul legislation after the event; and that one of the two censors must be a plebeian. In 336 he became the first plebeian praetor, despite the presiding consul's objection, and in 332 he was censor.

In his second consulship (327) he besieged Neapolis and Palaepolis, and when his year ended the people voted to extend his command 'in place of a consul' (pro consule) until the siege was finished: the first prorogation of imperium, the device that later made possible Rome's overseas commands. He captured the city in 326, after which Neapolis received a favourable treaty, and celebrated the first triumph by a proconsul. He was consul again in 320 and 315, serving with Papirius Cursor in the years after the Caudine Forks.

Philo's career shows how quickly the plebeian elite integrated into the leadership of the state after 367. His laws of 339 are part of the series (449, 339, 287) that gradually made the plebeian assembly sovereign; modern scholars debate what each added. His prorogation transformed the annual magistracy into a flexible instrument for long wars.

L. Papirius Cursor was the Roman general most admired by the annalists for the Second Samnite War. He was consul five times (326, 320, 319, 315, 313) and dictator twice (325 and 309). His cognomen 'the runner' was said to come from his speed of foot; he was also known for an enormous appetite, physical strength and an iron discipline that made him feared by his soldiers. Livy tells that he once ordered his lictor to prepare the axe for a Praenestine praetor who had been slow, then had him merely cut a tree root before dismissing him.

As dictator in 325 he left his master of horse Q. Fabius Rullianus in command with orders not to engage; Fabius fought and won at Imbrinium, and Papirius demanded his execution for disobedience. Fabius fled to Rome, and only the pleas of his father, the Senate and the people persuaded Papirius to pardon him, while insisting that military authority had been upheld. After the Caudine Forks, as consul in 320 and 319, he was credited with retaking Luceria, recovering the 600 hostages and sending 7,000 Samnites under the yoke, a story many modern historians reject. As dictator in 309 he won the battle in which the Samnites fought with gilded and silvered shields, and he triumphed.

Livy uses Papirius in his famous digression on Alexander the Great, arguing that had Alexander invaded Italy he would have met generals like Papirius, Fabius, Valerius Corvus and Manlius, and been defeated. His son of the same name, consul in 293 and 272, won at Aquilonia and took Tarentum. The Papirii were a patrician house whose prestige rested heavily on these two men.

Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus (or Rullus) was the greatest Roman commander of the Samnite wars and the founder of the Fabii Maximi. As master of horse in 325 he fought and won at Imbrinium against the dictator Papirius Cursor's orders, and was nearly executed. He was consul five times (322, 310, 308, 297, 295), dictator in 315, when he was defeated by the Samnites at Lautulae, and censor in 304, and was princeps senatus.

His campaign of 310 made his name. With Sutrium besieged by the Etruscans, he sent his brother, raised at Caere and fluent in Etruscan, disguised as a peasant through the dense Ciminian forest, then marched his army through it into central Etruria, where no Roman army had been, ravaged the land and won at Perusia, provoking the Senate's alarm and then its admiration. In 308 he defeated the Umbrians at Mevania. As censor in 304 he undid Appius Claudius' distribution of humble citizens and freedmen among all the tribes, confining them to the four urban tribes, which earned him the cognomen Maximus, and he instituted the annual parade of the equites on 15 July. In 295, at nearly 70, he commanded with Decius Mus at Sentinum, where his patience and use of reserves won the battle after his colleague's death, and vowed a temple to Jupiter Victor. In 292 he served as legate to his son, Q. Fabius Gurges, and shared in the capture of Gavius Pontius.

Livy's account of him is shaped by the family historian Fabius Pictor, and Diodorus sometimes contradicts the Fabian victories. The Esquiline painting naming a Q. Fabius may show him. His great-grandson Q. Fabius Maximus Cunctator, the opponent of Hannibal, inherited his cognomen and a family tradition of cautious generalship.

Gavius Pontius, son of Herennius, commanded the Samnite army in 321 and inflicted on Rome its most humiliating defeat before Cannae. Learning that the Roman consuls were camped near Calatia, he sent soldiers disguised as shepherds to tell them that the Samnites were besieging Luceria, lured them through the Caudine pass and trapped them between blocked defiles. Livy gives him eloquent speeches: before the war, protesting that the Samnites had offered every satisfaction and that the gods would favour the side wronged; at Caudium, consulting his aged father, who advised him either to free the Romans without humiliation or to kill them all. Pontius chose the middle course, making the consuls and the army pass under the yoke and taking 600 equites as hostages.

When Rome repudiated the agreement and handed over the consul Sp. Postumius and the other guarantors, Pontius refused to accept them, denouncing the Romans for mocking the gods with legal tricks and offering to return the army to the pass if they wished to cancel the peace. Livy then makes him suffer defeat and the yoke at Luceria, which modern scholars largely reject.

A Gavius Pontius commanded the Samnites again in 292 against Q. Fabius Gurges; captured, he was led in Fabius' triumph in 291 and executed, a breach of the usual Roman custom of sparing kings that later writers condemned. Whether this was the same man, thirty years after Caudium, or a son is uncertain. Cicero quotes a saying attributed to Pontius that he wished he had been born when the Romans accepted bribes, for then he would not have let them rule. In Samnite memory he remained the national hero; the Pontii of the late Republic, such as Pontius Telesinus who fought Sulla at the Colline Gate in 82, claimed his tradition.

Ap. Claudius Caecus ('the Blind') was the most original Roman statesman before the Punic wars. His career, recorded in an elogium set up in the Forum of Augustus, included three military tribunates, the quaestorship, two curule aedileships, two praetorships, the censorship (312), two consulships (307 and 296), a dictatorship and three interregna. As censor with C. Plautius he built the Via Appia to Capua and the Aqua Appia, Rome's first aqueduct, carrying water 16.4 km, mostly underground, from springs near the Via Praenestina to the Forum Boarium; he enrolled sons of freedmen in the Senate and distributed the landless and freedmen among all the tribes, increasing their voting weight; he transferred the cult of Hercules at the Ara Maxima from the Potitii to public slaves; and he refused to resign after eighteen months, holding office, by some accounts, for nearly five years until his roads and aqueduct were finished.

As consul in 296 he fought in Etruria and Samnium and vowed the temple of Bellona, in front of which stood the column from which the fetials threw a spear to declare war. His scribe Gnaeus Flavius published the legal formulas and the calendar of court days. Blind in old age, he had himself carried into the Senate in 280 when it was inclined to accept Pyrrhus' peace offer through Cineas, and delivered a speech that persuaded it to refuse while Pyrrhus remained in Italy; Cicero knew the speech in writing. He is the first Roman author whose works were known later: a collection of moral maxims in verse ('every man is the maker of his own fortune' is attributed to him), a legal treatise, and spelling reforms, including the rhotacism that turned intervocalic s into r (Valesii into Valerii) and the removal of the letter z.

Mommsen saw him as a democratic reformer; others see a Hellenising aristocrat who built a personal clientele among the urban population. The contradictions of his censorship, combining public works on an unprecedented scale with the defiance of convention, anticipate later popular politicians.

M'. Curius Dentatus, a plebeian new man probably from the Sabine borderland, was the hero of the final conquest of central Italy and the Pyrrhic war. Pliny says he was born with teeth, hence Dentatus. As tribune of the plebs, perhaps around 298, he forced the patrician senators to approve in advance the election of a plebeian consul whom the interrex Appius Claudius refused. As consul in 290 he ended the Third Samnite War and in the same year conquered the Sabines and the Praetuttii, celebrating two triumphs; the Sabine land was so extensive that he said he had taken more land than could be cultivated and more people than could be fed. He distributed it in allotments of seven iugera, saying that anyone not content with seven iugera was a dangerous citizen. He drained the Lacus Velinus by cutting a channel to the Nar, creating the Marmore falls and a long dispute between Reate and Interamna.

Suffect consul in 284 after the death of Metellus at Arretium, and praetor in 283, he was consul again in 275, when he defeated Pyrrhus near Maleventum and triumphed with the first elephants seen at Rome, and in 274. When a citizen failed to answer his levy he sold first his goods and then the man. As censor in 272 he used the Pyrrhic spoils to build the Anio Vetus aqueduct, and he died in 270 while serving on the commission to complete it.

His poverty became legend: Samnite envoys found him roasting turnips at his hearth and offered gold, which he refused, saying he preferred to rule those who had gold. Cato the Elder, whose farm lay near Curius' cottage in the Sabine country, made him his personal model, and Curius became a byword for old Roman frugality in Cicero, Horace and Juvenal.

C. Fabricius Luscinus, a plebeian new man, perhaps from the Hernican town of Aletrium, became the Roman model of incorruptibility. As consul in 282 he relieved Thurii, besieged by the Lucanians and Bruttii, and triumphed over them and the Samnites; the grateful Thurians set up his statue in Rome. In 280, after Heraclea, he went as envoy to Pyrrhus to negotiate the release of prisoners. The king offered him gold, which he refused, and the next day tried to frighten him with an elephant hidden behind a curtain; Fabricius said that neither the gold of yesterday nor the beast of today moved him. Pyrrhus released the prisoners on parole for the Saturnalia, and all returned.

As consul again in 278, he received a letter from Pyrrhus' doctor offering to poison the king for a reward, and sent it to Pyrrhus with a warning, telling him that Rome wished to win by arms, not crime; Pyrrhus, according to Eutropius, said it would be easier to turn the sun from its course than Fabricius from honour, and released the prisoners without ransom. In the same year Fabricius negotiated the remarkably favourable treaty with Heraclea and triumphed over the Lucanians, Bruttii, Tarentines and Samnites. As censor in 275 he expelled the twice-consul P. Cornelius Rufinus from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate.

His poverty was proverbial: he owned only a silver salt-cellar and a small dish with a horn foot; the state provided his daughter's dowry; and his family was granted burial within the city. Pyrrhus, Cineas' Epicureanism and Fabricius' reply made a favourite theme of moralists. Rousseau's 'prosopopoeia of Fabricius' in his Discourse on the Arts and Sciences (1750), imagining his ghost appalled by Roman luxury, made him a symbol of republican virtue for the Enlightenment.

Pyrrhus (319-272), king of the Molossians and hegemon of Epirus, claimed descent from Achilles' son Neoptolemus. Exiled as a child, he fought for Demetrius Poliorcetes at Ipsus (301), lived as a hostage at the court of Ptolemy I, married his stepdaughter Antigone, and with Ptolemy's support regained his throne in 297. He enlarged Epirus with Ambracia, Acarnania and Corcyra, the dowry of his wife Lanassa, daughter of Agathocles, and was briefly king of half of Macedonia (288-284) until Lysimachus drove him out.

In 281 Tarentum invited him against Rome. He landed in 280 with about 25,000 men and 20 elephants, imposed martial discipline on the Tarentines, and defeated the Romans at Heraclea and, at heavy cost, at Ausculum (279). His envoy Cineas offered peace but the Senate, roused by the blind Appius Claudius, refused to negotiate while he stood in Italy. In 278 he accepted the Sicilian Greeks' invitation against Carthage, took Eryx and most of the island but failed before Lilybaeum, and alienated the Sicilians with his autocracy. Returning to Italy in 276, he lost ships to the Carthaginians in the Strait, plundered Locri's temple treasure, and was checked by M'. Curius near Maleventum (275). He left for Greece, defeated Antigonus Gonatas, failed to take Sparta, and was killed in a street fight in Argos in 272, struck by a roof tile thrown by an old woman.

He wrote memoirs and military treatises used by later generals, and Hannibal, according to Plutarch and Livy, ranked him first or second among commanders. Antigonus compared him to a dice-player who makes good throws but does not know how to use them. For Rome his war was decisive: it brought Rome into contact with Hellenistic warfare, elephants and diplomacy, proved that Roman manpower could outlast the best professional army, and left Rome master of Italy. 'Pyrrhic victory' preserves his remark after Ausculum.

Cineas of Thessaly, a pupil of Demosthenes and the best orator of his time according to Plutarch, was Pyrrhus' chief adviser and envoy. Pyrrhus said that Cineas had won him more cities by his words than he had taken by arms. Plutarch's famous dialogue has Cineas ask the king what he will do after conquering Rome; then Sicily; then Carthage and Africa; then Macedonia and Greece; and when Pyrrhus answers that he will then relax and enjoy himself with his friends, Cineas asks what prevents him doing that now.

After Heraclea, Pyrrhus sent Cineas to Rome with an offer of peace and alliance: Rome would recognise the freedom of Tarentum and the Italiote Greeks and restore what it had taken from the Samnites, Lucanians, Bruttii and Apulians. Cineas, who had memorised the names of the senators and leading equites within a day of his arrival and greeted them individually, brought gifts for the senators and their wives, which were refused. The Senate was inclined to accept until the blind Appius Claudius had himself carried in and declared that Rome would not negotiate while a foreign king stood on Italian soil. Cineas returned with the report that the Senate seemed to him an assembly of kings, and that fighting the Romans was like fighting the Hydra, since their manpower was inexhaustible. He also introduced Fabricius to Epicurean doctrine at Pyrrhus' table, provoking the Roman's wish that Rome's enemies should adopt it.

Cineas went ahead to Sicily in 278 to prepare Pyrrhus' campaign there and disappears from the record soon after. He also wrote an epitome of the military writer Aeneas Tacticus, which Cicero mentions. His sayings, preserved by Plutarch, Appian and Justin, gave the Greek world its first images of Roman political character.

Dionysius I (c. 432-367), the son of Hermocritus, rose from clerk to tyrant of Syracuse in 405, exploiting the panic after Carthage destroyed Acragas. He ruled for 38 years, the longest and most successful tyranny in Greek history, and built the greatest power of the Greek world in his time. He made the island of Ortygia a fortified palace-citadel, enclosed the plateau of Epipolae with a wall of about 27 km and the fortress of Euryalus, and hired mercenaries from Campania, Gaul, Iberia and Greece. His engineers developed the first catapults (399) and he built quadriremes and quinqueremes, larger warships than any before.

He fought Carthage four times. In 397 he besieged and destroyed Motya; in 396 he survived Himilco's siege of Syracuse; around 378-375 he won at Cabala but lost heavily at Cronium; and in 368 he attacked Lilybaeum. In Italy he allied with the Lucanians, crushed the Italiote League at the Elleporus (389), destroyed Caulonia and Hipponion and starved Rhegium into surrender (387), took Croton (379) and founded or supported colonies on the Adriatic (Issa, Lissus, Pharos, Ancona). In 384 his fleet sacked the sanctuary of Pyrgi, the port of Caere, carrying off treasure worth about 1,000 talents, and Justin says he received an embassy from the Gauls who had sacked Rome. His career thus touched Rome's world directly.

Ancient anecdotes depict a suspicious despot: he married two wives on the same day, the Locrian Doris and the Syracusan Aristomache; he had his daughters shave him with hot walnut shells; and Cicero tells how he showed the courtier Damocles the happiness of a tyrant by seating him at a banquet beneath a sword hanging by a single hair. He was also a tragic poet, crowned at the Lenaea in Athens shortly before his death. Plato's visit around 388 began the troubled connection between the Academy and Syracuse.

Agathocles (361-289), born at Thermae Himeraeae, son of a potter who settled in Syracuse under Timoleon's resettlement, rose as a soldier, was twice exiled, served as a mercenary captain in southern Italy, and in 317, backed by the Carthaginian general Hamilcar, seized power in Syracuse through a massacre of the oligarchs. He promised cancellation of debts and redistribution of land and was elected general with full powers.

After years of war with the other Sicilian cities and Carthage, he was defeated at the Himeras in 311 and besieged in Syracuse. In a stroke of strategic audacity he broke out with 60 ships in August 310, under a total eclipse, landed at Cape Bon, burned his ships as an offering to Demeter and Kore so that his men could not retreat, and carried the war to Africa. He beat the Carthaginians at White Tunis, ravaged the rich estates of the Punic countryside, took Utica and other towns, and murdered his ally Ophellas of Cyrene to take over his army. Carthage, meanwhile, was shaken by Bomilcar's attempted coup. But in 307, after defeats of his son Archagathus, Agathocles fled back to Sicily, leaving his sons to be killed by the army. A peace in 306 restored the old frontiers. In 304 he took the title of king, married a stepdaughter of Ptolemy I and gave his daughter Lanassa to Pyrrhus with Corcyra as dowry. In his last years he campaigned in southern Italy, taking Croton and Hipponion. He died in 289, perhaps poisoned, refusing to name a successor.

Timaeus, whom he exiled, wrote a ferociously hostile history; Polybius, though critical of Timaeus' bias, reported that Scipio Africanus named Agathocles and Dionysius as the men who combined boldness and prudence best. His African invasion became a model for Regulus and for Scipio, and his discharged Campanian mercenaries, the Mamertines, seized Messana and triggered the First Punic War.

Timoleon (c. 411-337), a Corinthian aristocrat, was known in his youth for having saved his brother Timophanes' life in battle and then, when Timophanes made himself tyrant of Corinth around 365, for consenting to his killing; shunned by his mother and tormented by guilt, he lived in retirement for twenty years. In 344, when Syracusan exiles appealed to their mother city against the tyrant Dionysius II and against Carthage, Corinth sent Timoleon with ten ships and a few hundred mercenaries.

He evaded the Carthaginian fleet at Rhegium, defeated Hicetas of Leontini at Adranum, received the surrender of Dionysius II, who retired to Corinth, and took over Ortygia, where he demolished the tyrants' citadel and built law courts on its site. In 339 (or 341), with perhaps 12,000 men, he surprised a large Carthaginian army crossing the river Crimissus in western Sicily in a thunderstorm and destroyed it, including the Sacred Band of 2,500 Carthaginian citizens. The peace that followed confirmed the Halycus river as the boundary of the Punic province. He then expelled or executed the remaining tyrants, including Hicetas and Mamercus of Catana, invited settlers from Greece (Plutarch claims 60,000) to repopulate the Sicilian cities, refounded Acragas and Gela, and gave Syracuse a revised constitution with an annual priest of Zeus Olympios as eponym.

Then, his sight failing, he retired as a private citizen, consulted on great matters, and died in 337/336; the Syracusans gave him a public funeral, annual games and a gymnasium called the Timoleonteion. Plutarch, using Timaeus, presents him as a liberator favoured by Fortune and pairs him with Aemilius Paullus. Archaeology confirms a remarkable late-4th-century revival of Greek Sicily, with new building and abundant Pegasus coinage, which lasted until Agathocles.

Lucretia, daughter of Sp. Lucretius Tricipitinus and wife of L. Tarquinius Collatinus, is the central figure of the foundation legend of the Republic. When the young princes at the siege of Ardea wagered on their wives' virtue and rode home by night, they found the king's daughters-in-law feasting, and Lucretia late at night spinning wool among her maids. Her beauty and chastity inflamed Sextus Tarquinius, who returned days later as a guest and, threatening to kill her and lay a dead slave beside her to make it appear she had been caught in adultery, raped her. She sent for her father and husband, each to come with a trusted friend; they came with P. Valerius and L. Junius Brutus. She told them what had happened, made them swear to avenge her, declared that though she absolved herself of guilt she would not be freed from punishment, so that no unchaste woman should live by her example, and stabbed herself. Her body, displayed in the forum of Collatia and in Rome, roused the people against the Tarquins.

For Livy and Ovid she was the supreme exemplum of pudicitia, the Roman matron's chastity, whose violation by a tyrant justified revolution, as the Verginia story would justify the fall of the decemvirs. Augustine, in the City of God, challenged the Roman admiration: if she was innocent, her suicide was the killing of an innocent woman; if she consented, she was not admirable. The story mirrors Greek tales in which sexual outrage triggers the fall of tyranny, notably the Athenian tyrannicides.

Lucretia became one of the most represented women of antiquity in later culture: Shakespeare's narrative poem The Rape of Lucrece (1594), paintings by Botticelli, Titian, Cranach, Artemisia Gentileschi and Rembrandt, and Benjamin Britten's opera The Rape of Lucretia (1946). Modern scholarship (Donaldson, Joshel) reads the legend as a meditation on the female body as the site of political order.

L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus ('the Bearded'), consul in 298, censor perhaps in 280, and great-grandfather of Scipio Africanus, is the earliest Roman whose own funerary monument survives. His peperino sarcophagus, the oldest burial in the Tomb of the Scipios on the Via Appia, was found in 1780 and is now in the Vatican Museums. Its form, with a Doric frieze of triglyphs and rosettes and Ionic volutes on the lid, is a Roman adaptation of Greek altar design. The inscription, in Saturnian verse, reads in archaic Latin: 'Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus, offspring of his father Gnaeus, a brave and wise man, whose appearance was most equal to his virtue, who was consul, censor and aedile among you; he took Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium, subdued all Lucania and led away hostages.'

Livy tells a different story for 298: that Barbatus campaigned in Etruria, fighting an indecisive battle near Volaterrae, while his colleague Cn. Fulvius fought in Samnium. Livy also places Barbatus as a legate in the campaigns of 297 and 295. The conflict between elogium and narrative is one of the classic problems of early Roman historiography: either Livy's sources confused the consuls' provinces, or the family elogium claimed successes of others. The verse elogium itself was probably inscribed after the original painted text was erased, perhaps around 200, and is thus a product of family memory a century after his death.

Barbatus' descendants, including his son L. Scipio, consul in 259 and conqueror of Corsica, whose own elogium survives, made the Cornelii Scipiones the most powerful family of the 3rd and 2nd centuries. The tomb, with its later facade adorned by statues that Livy believed included the poet Ennius, was a monument to the family's claim on Rome's history.

Gelon (c. 540-478), son of Deinomenes, belonged to a family of hereditary priests of Demeter and Kore from Gela. He commanded the cavalry of Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, and on Hippocrates' death in 491 seized power for himself. In 485, called in by the exiled landowners of Syracuse, he took the city, made it his capital, left Gela to his brother Hiero and transformed Syracuse by transplanting populations: the people of Camarina, half of Gela, and the rich of Megara Hyblaea and Sicilian Euboea were made Syracusans, while the poor of Megara were sold abroad. He married Damarete, daughter of Theron of Acragas, and built a fleet and army that made him the most powerful Greek ruler of his day.

When the Greek allies asked his help against Xerxes in 481 he offered 200 triremes, 20,000 hoplites and supplies on condition that he command on land or sea, which Sparta and Athens refused. In 480 Carthage, called in by Terillus of Himera and Anaxilas of Rhegium, sent Hamilcar with a great army; Gelon and Theron destroyed it at Himera. Hamilcar died, according to Herodotus by throwing himself into the sacrificial fire. Greek tradition synchronised Himera with Salamis (Herodotus) or Thermopylae (Diodorus), making it the western half of the Greek victory over the barbarians. The peace imposed on Carthage brought 2,000 talents; Gelon built temples to Demeter and Kore, and dedicated a golden tripod and Nike at Delphi and treasures at Olympia.

He died of dropsy in 478 and was honoured as a hero; his brother Hiero succeeded. Diodorus, drawing on Timaeus, paints him as a model ruler who presented himself unarmed before the Syracusan assembly. His victory secured Greek Sicily for seventy years and made the Syracusan state the partner and rival of Carthage that Rome would confront two centuries later.

The first years of the Republic were spent fighting off the exiled Tarquins and their Etruscan allies. In 509 Veii and Tarquinii marched on Rome; in the battle at the Silva Arsia the consul Brutus and Arruns, son of Tarquin, killed each other in single combat, the battle was drawn, and in the night a voice from the forest, attributed to Silvanus, proclaimed that the Etruscans had lost one man more. P. Valerius triumphed. In 508 Lars Porsenna of Clusium, the most powerful Etruscan king of the day, attacked: Roman legend tells of Horatius at the bridge, Mucius Scaevola's burned hand and Cloelia's escape, after which Porsenna made peace in admiration, taking hostages and the land Rome had taken from Veii.

Non-Roman evidence suggests the reality was harsher. Tacitus speaks of the city's surrender to Porsenna, and Pliny quotes a treaty forbidding the Romans iron except for agriculture. Porsenna's power in Latium collapsed when his son Arruns besieged Aricia (504 in the traditional chronology) and was defeated and killed by the Latins and the Cumaean army of Aristodemus. Dionysius' account of this battle comes from a Cumaean chronicle independent of Roman tradition, and confirms the broad outline. Etruscan survivors who fled to Rome were settled in the Vicus Tuscus below the Palatine. Tarquin then moved to Tusculum, where his son-in-law Octavius Mamilius was building the Latin coalition that fought at Lake Regillus.

Modern historians read the war as part of the collapse of Etruscan hegemony in Latium and Campania at the end of the 6th century: Etruscan defeat at Aricia (504) was followed by the naval defeat at Cumae (474). Rome emerged independent, but weaker than under the kings, and needed a generation to rebuild its position among the Latins. Some scholars think Porsenna, not the Roman aristocracy, removed Tarquin, and that the Republic was born under Clusine supervision.

After the fall of the monarchy Rome lost the hegemony over Latium that the first treaty with Carthage assumes. The Latin cities met in council at the grove and spring of Ferentina near Aricia, and Dionysius preserves a list of about thirty Latin peoples who swore alliance against Rome, among them Ardea, Aricia, Lanuvium, Lavinium, Tibur, Tusculum, Praeneste, Gabii, Velitrae, Norba, Circeii, Cora, Satricum and Corioli. Their leader was Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, son-in-law of Tarquinius Superbus, who sheltered the old king. Cato's fragment on the dedication of the grove of Diana at Aricia by a Tusculan 'Latin dictator' may belong to this coalition.

Rome's response included the first dictatorship (501 or 498), the capture of Crustumerium and the defection of Praeneste to Rome (499). The decisive battle was fought at Lake Regillus in Tusculan territory, in 499 or 496, under the dictator A. Postumius Albus. Mamilius was killed, the Tarquins' last army destroyed, and the old king fled to Cumae, where he died in 495; legend added the epiphany of Castor and Pollux, whose temple in the Forum was dedicated in 484.

The war did not end in Roman domination. The rise of the Volsci and Aequi, who were pressing into the Pontine plain and the Alban hills, gave both sides reasons to reconcile, and in 493 Sp. Cassius concluded the Foedus Cassianum, a treaty of perpetual peace and mutual defence between Rome and the Latins on equal terms, with shared booty and joint colonies. The Hernici joined in 486. The alliance, renewed in 358, lasted until the Latin revolt of 340. Historians debate how equal it really was, but the first Latin war established the framework of Roman-Latin relations that underpinned Rome's survival in the 5th century.

The Volsci, an Oscan-Umbrian people whose language is known from the 3rd-century Tabula Veliterna, descended from the uplands of the Liris and Sacco valleys around 500 and took over much of southern Latium: Antium, Satricum, Velitrae, Suessa Pometia, Anxur (Tarracina), Privernum, Circeii, Ecetra and Corioli. Their arrival, part of the wider movement of Sabellian peoples out of the Apennines that also brought Samnites into Campania and Lucanians into the south, threatened Rome and the Latins equally, and was a main reason for the Foedus Cassianum.

The wars fall into phases. From 495 to the 460s Rome and the Latins fought for the Pontine plain: Suessa Pometia (502, 495), Corioli (493), Coriolanus' march on Rome (488), the capture of Antium (468) and the colony there (467). Through the mid-5th century the Volsci and their Aequian allies raided Latium almost yearly by the Algidus pass, and Livy's narrative of these 'Volscian and Aequian' campaigns is repetitive and partly fictitious. The tide turned with Rome's victory on the Algidus (431), and in 406 Rome took Anxur. After the Gallic sack the Volsci revived, with Latin cities such as Velitrae and Circeii joining them; Camillus fought them at Maecium (389) and Satricum (386, 381), the colonies at Satricum, Setia, Sutrium and Nepet secured the frontier, and the Pomptine tribe was created on Volscian land in 358. Valerius Corvus burned Satricum in 346, and the Volsci joined the Latin revolt of 340.

The end came in 338, when Antium's fleet was destroyed and its beaks fixed to the Rostra, and in 329, when Privernum fell after a siege; its envoys' famous reply, that they would keep faithfully a good peace but not a bad one, won them citizenship. The Volscian country became Roman territory, with citizen colonies at Antium and Tarracina and the Oufentina tribe (318). A century and a half of warfare had turned the southern edge of Latium into the base for Rome's advance into Campania.

The Aequi inhabited the valleys of the upper Anio and Turano and the highlands around Carseoli and the Fucine lake, east of Tibur and Praeneste. Their raids came down through the Algidus pass between the Alban hills and the Praenestine mountains, threatening Tusculum, Labici and the approaches to Rome, often in concert with the Volsci. For most of the 5th century the Aequian war was a seasonal struggle for the Algidus.

Livy's narrative records repeated crises: in 465 and 464 consular armies were nearly trapped; in 458 the Aequi under Gracchus Cloelius surrounded the consul L. Minucius on the Algidus, and Cincinnatus, called from his plough, relieved him and sent the Aequi under the yoke; in 449 the decemvirs' army was beaten; in 446 the Aequi and Volsci raided up to the Esquiline Gate. The decisive victory came in 431, when the dictator A. Postumius Tubertus defeated a combined Aequian and Volscian army on the Algidus, after which Rome took the offensive, planting a colony at Labici (418) and fighting for Bolae (415-414). After the Gallic sack the Aequi were a lesser threat.

The end was brutal. After the Second Samnite War, in 304, the consuls P. Sempronius Sophus and P. Sulpicius Saverrio invaded Aequian territory and, according to Livy, stormed 31 towns in 50 days, most of which were burned; 'the name of the Aequi was nearly annihilated'. Latin colonies were planted at Alba Fucens (303, with 6,000 settlers) and Carseoli (298), and the road later known as the Via Valeria secured the route through their land to the Marsi and the Adriatic. The neighbouring Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini and Frentani, watching, sought treaties with Rome. A remnant, the Aequiculi, survived around Nersae. The fate of the Aequi became a lesson in what awaited peoples who resisted Rome to the end.

Veii, the great Etruscan city 15 km north of Rome, controlled the right bank of the lower Tiber, the salt pans at its mouth, and the bridgehead of Fidenae on the left bank. The first war of the Republic with Veii (483-474) was fought over these routes. After years of raids, in 480 the consuls M. Fabius and Cn. Manlius fought a costly battle before Veii in which the former consul Q. Fabius and the consul Manlius were killed. The Fabii then made the war their own: in 479, according to Livy, 306 men of the Fabian gens, with their clients (4,000 according to Dionysius), marched out through the right-hand arch of the Porta Carmentalis and built a fort on the Cremera, a tributary of the Tiber below Veii, from which they raided Veientine territory for two years. In 477 they were lured into an ambush and annihilated; only one boy, left at home, survived to continue the family. Ovid dates the disaster to 13 February, Livy to 18 July, the day of the Allia.

The Veientes exploited the disaster, occupied the Janiculum and crossed the Tiber; fighting at the temple of Spes and the Colline Gate and a grain shortage followed, until in 476 they were dislodged. The tribunes prosecuted the consul T. Menenius for failing to relieve the Fabii. In 474, after a further Roman victory, Veii obtained a forty-year truce.

The Cremera story is surely embellished. The figure of 306 Fabii echoes the 300 Spartans at Thermopylae, fought in the same years, and the family tradition was transmitted by Fabius Pictor. But a private war fought by an aristocratic clan with its retainers fits the world of the Lapis Satricanus, where a Valerius' 'companions' dedicate to Mars, and many historians accept that the early Republic's wars were partly conducted by gentilicial war bands. The truce of 474 coincided with Syracuse's naval victory over the Etruscans at Cumae, a sign of declining Etruscan power.

The second war with Veii (438-425) began with the defection of Fidenae, the Tiber-crossing town 8 km north of Rome, which had received Roman colonists, to Lars Tolumnius, king of Veii. The Fidenates killed four Roman envoys at Tolumnius' prompting, an outrage commemorated by their statues on the Rostra. In 437 the dictator Mam. Aemilius and his master of horse fought the Veientes, Fidenates and Faliscans below Fidenae, and A. Cornelius Cossus, then a military tribune, killed Tolumnius in single combat and dedicated his armour to Jupiter Feretrius: the spolia opima, won only three times in Roman history (Romulus, Cossus and Marcellus in 222).

Cossus' rank became a political issue under Augustus. Livy reports that Augustus, restoring the temple of Jupiter Feretrius, saw Cossus' linen corslet inscribed with the title of consul, which implied the spolia were won in his consulship of 428, not as a tribune in 437. The point mattered because in 29 BC M. Licinius Crassus, proconsul of Macedonia, claimed the spolia opima for killing a Bastarnian king, and Augustus, by insisting that only a commander fighting under his own auspices could dedicate them, blocked the claim.

Plague slowed the war in the 430s, while the Etruscan council at the Fanum Voltumnae refused Veii help (434). In 426 Fidenae revolted again and massacred its Roman colonists; the dictator Mam. Aemilius took it, Livy says by driving a tunnel into its citadel, sold the inhabitants and destroyed the town. In 425 Veii accepted a twenty-year truce. The war gave Rome the whole left bank of the lower Tiber and its crossing points, preparing the final war with Veii twenty years later.

When the truce of 425 expired, Veii refused Rome's demands for redress, and in 406 the war began that ended with the city's destruction. It was a different kind of war from the seasonal raids of the 5th century. Pay for soldiers, funded by a property tax, was introduced in 406; the army wintered before Veii for the first time in 403; citizens of equestrian rank volunteered to serve on their own horses. The siege lines, as Livy describes them, included camps, ramparts and siege works. Veii's allies, Capena and the Faliscans, attacked the lines in 402, exploiting the quarrel of the consular tribunes M'. Sergius and L. Verginius, and the camp was lost. The Etruscan league at the Fanum Voltumnae refused to help, partly because Veii had chosen a king whom the other cities disliked.

The religious narrative dominates the last years: the rising of the Alban Lake (398), the oracle from Delphi and a Veientine prophecy that the city would fall when the lake was drained, the drainage tunnel, and the dictatorship of M. Furius Camillus in 396, who took the city by mining under its citadel and called out its goddess Juno Regina. The population was sold, the booty divided, a tenth vowed to Apollo, and a golden bowl sent to Delphi, which was intercepted by pirates from Lipara and restored by their magistrate Timasitheus, honoured by Rome with hospitium.

Capena surrendered in 395 and Falerii in 394. The Veientine territory was distributed in seven-iugera plots and organised in four new tribes in 387, raising Rome's territory from about 820 to some 1,500 km2 by Beloch's estimate. Rome had destroyed a major Etruscan city for the first time, and its manpower and land were now greater than any Latin or Etruscan rival's. The victory was nearly lost six years later when the Gauls sacked Rome, and there was serious debate about moving the whole people to Veii.

Celtic peoples had been crossing the Alps into the Po valley for generations; Livy dates the first migration to the reign of Tarquinius Priscus, Polybius describes the settlement of the Insubres, Boii, Lingones and finally the Senones on the Adriatic coast. Early in the 4th century they overwhelmed the Etruscan cities north of the Apennines (Melpum fell in 396, in the same year as Veii according to Nepos). In 391 a band of Senones under Brennus crossed into Etruria and besieged Clusium; Livy repeats a story that a Clusine noble, Arruns, had invited them in revenge on a seducer, luring them with wine.

Rome sent three envoys, sons of M. Fabius Ambustus, to mediate. When they fought in the Clusine ranks and one killed a Gallic chief, the Gauls demanded their surrender; the Roman people instead elected them consular tribunes. The Gauls marched south, routed the Roman army at the Allia on 18 July, and entered the undefended city three days later. They plundered and burned it but failed to take the Capitol, which held out for seven months until the defenders, starving, paid 1,000 pounds of gold. Livy has Camillus arrive at that moment and destroy the Gauls; Polybius says they left because the Veneti were attacking their homeland, and Diodorus and Strabo that the Caeretans defeated them on the way back.

Polybius' synchronism with the Peace of Antalcidas and Dionysius' siege of Rhegium puts the sack in 387/386, about four years after the Varronian 390. The war exposed Rome's weakness: Latin and Volscian allies revolted, the Etruscans attacked Sutrium, and there was debate about abandoning the city for Veii. Caere, which sheltered the Vestals, received a special relationship with Rome. The long-term responses were the stone wall of 378, the manipular army, the special Gallic treasury, and a fear of the Gauls that shaped Roman policy until Caesar's conquest of Gaul.

After 390 Gallic bands returned repeatedly to Latium, perhaps moving between the Po valley, central Italy and Apulia, where some may have served as mercenaries for Dionysius of Syracuse. Livy records a sequence of invasions and Roman victories, each with a heroic episode. In 367 Camillus, dictator for the fifth time, defeated Gauls near Alba, his last victory. In 361 the Gauls camped by the Anio bridge on the Via Salaria, and young T. Manlius killed a giant Gallic champion and took his torque, earning the name Torquatus. In 360 Gauls operating from Tibur, which allied with them, reached the Colline Gate and were driven off by the dictator Q. Servilius Ahala. In 358 the dictator C. Sulpicius Peticus won near Pedum and deposited the gold from the booty in a stone vault on the Capitol. In 350 the plebeian consul M. Popillius Laenas, fighting wounded, defeated a large Gallic army in Latium. In 349 M. Valerius, aided by a raven, killed another champion, and the consul L. Furius Camillus drove the Gauls out of the Pomptine territory, while a Greek fleet raided the coast at the same time.

Polybius' briefer account has a different rhythm: twelve years after the sack the Gauls returned with a great army and the Romans did not dare to meet them; thirty years later the Romans, with their allies, were ready and the Gauls withdrew; and after thirteen more years the Gauls, seeing Roman power, made a peace that held for thirty years. Livy's sequence may combine real raids with family legends of single combats.

The wars mattered beyond their scale. They tested the reorganised army, gave plebeian consuls like Popillius their first victories, revealed the unreliability of Tibur and Praeneste, and taught the Romans to fight Celtic warriors, whose initial charge they learned to withstand. Roman-Gallic peace, probably formalised with the Senones around 331, freed Rome for the Samnite wars.

In 358 Tarquinii, the leading city of southern Etruria and once the seat of the Tarquin family's ancestors, attacked Roman territory, joined by the Faliscans. The consul C. Fabius Ambustus was defeated, and the Tarquinians sacrificed 307 Roman prisoners in their forum, an act Livy records with horror and that recalls the Etruscan funerary scenes of prisoner sacrifice, such as the François Tomb at Vulci. In 357 the Faliscans joined openly. In 356 the Etruscans advanced to the salt works at the mouth of the Tiber, and C. Marcius Rutilus, the first plebeian dictator, defeated them, capturing 8,000 men, and triumphed by popular vote against the Senate's will.

The war continued. In 354 Rome took its revenge for 358, scourging and beheading 358 Tarquinian nobles in the Forum. In 353 Caere, Rome's old friend that had sheltered the Vestals in 390, joined Tarquinii and raided the salt works, then sued for peace when Rome declared war, and in memory of its service in 390 received a hundred-year truce. In 351, their lands ravaged, Tarquinii and Falerii obtained forty-year truces.

The war shows Rome's growing pressure on southern Etruria after the conquest of Veii, and the vulnerability of the salt trade and the Tiber mouth. The Elogia Tarquiniensia, Latin inscriptions of the 1st century AD honouring the Spurinnae, may commemorate Tarquinian leaders of this period, including an Aulus Spurinna who deposed a king of Caere and fought Arretium. Painted tombs of 4th-century Tarquinii, such as the Tomba dell'Orco and Tomba degli Scudi, show an aristocracy of magistrates (zilath) proud of their families and offices, the class whom Rome would later bind to itself as allies.

In 343 the Samnites, the federation of highland peoples of the central-southern Apennines, attacked the Sidicini of Teanum. The Sidicini turned to Capua, whose Campanian army was defeated by the Samnites on Mount Tifata and besieged. The Campanians appealed to Rome; the Senate hesitated because of its treaty with the Samnites (354), until the Campanians surrendered themselves and their city unconditionally to Rome (deditio), making their defence a Roman obligation. When the Samnites rejected Roman demands, war followed.

Livy describes three Roman victories in 343. M. Valerius Corvus defeated the Samnites at Mount Gaurus above Cumae, in a hard battle in which the Samnites complained that the Romans' eyes seemed to blaze; A. Cornelius Cossus, trapped near Saticula, was saved by the military tribune P. Decius Mus, who seized a hill above the enemy, and then won; and Valerius won again at Suessula. Both consuls triumphed, and Carthage sent a golden crown to Jupiter Capitolinus. In 342 the Roman garrison wintering in Campania plotted to seize Capua for themselves, as the Samnites had seized it from the Etruscans; the mutiny, quelled by the dictator Valerius Corvus with an amnesty, was followed by the Genucian laws. In 341 the consul L. Aemilius ravaged Samnium, and peace was made, renewing the old treaty and leaving the Sidicini to the Samnites.

Some scholars (notably Adcock, and with reservations Salmon) doubted much of this war, noting the difficulty of Capua's deditio and the oddness of Rome making peace so soon. Most now accept its outline. Its importance lay in what followed: Rome's abandonment of the Sidicini and its new hold on Capua alarmed the Latins and Campanians, who revolted in 340.

By 341 the Latins, allied to Rome since 493, saw the alliance becoming domination, while Rome's new hold on Capua and its peace with the Samnites threatened them further. The Latins, Campanians, Volscians of Antium and the Sidicini combined. Their spokesman, L. Annius of Setia, proposed to the Senate on the Capitol that one consul and half the Senate be Latin, so that Rome and Latium would form one state; Livy says Annius, insulting Jupiter, fell down the temple steps and was knocked senseless. War followed in 340.

The consuls T. Manlius Torquatus and P. Decius Mus marched, Livy says, through the Marsi and Paeligni to join the Samnites and met the Latin and Campanian army near Vesuvius. Before the battle Manlius executed his own son for fighting a duel against orders; in the battle Decius devoted himself to save the wavering left wing. A second victory at Trifanum, between Minturnae and Sinuessa, broke the Latins; the Campanians lost the Falernian territory, which was distributed to Roman settlers in small plots. In 339 Q. Publilius Philo won on the Fenectane plains while the siege of Pedum failed. In 338 L. Furius Camillus took Pedum and C. Maenius destroyed the Latin and Antiate fleet at the Astura, and Latium surrendered.

The settlement of 338 was the war's real result: the Latin League was dissolved, some cities incorporated with full citizenship, others given citizenship without the vote or kept as allies with separate treaties, Antium given a colony and its ships' beaks set on the Rostra. Rome now ruled a territorial state from southern Etruria to Campania, and the system of graded statuses created in 338 was extended to all of Italy over the following seventy years. The Latin demand for equal partnership, refused in 340, was finally granted, in a different form, after the Social War of 91-88.

The 'Great Samnite War' began over the Campanian coast and the middle Liris. Rome founded a Latin colony at Fregellae on the Liris in 328, on land the Samnites claimed, and in 327 intervened at Neapolis, where Samnite and Nolan garrisons had installed themselves. Q. Publilius Philo's siege, prolonged by the first prorogation of command, ended with the betrayal of the city and a favourable treaty (326). Rome gained the Lucanians and Apulians as allies, campaigned against the Vestini (325), and in 325 the master of horse Q. Fabius Rullianus won at Imbrinium against the dictator's orders. The Samnites surrendered the body of Brutulus Papius but Rome refused peace, and in 321 both consular armies surrendered at the Caudine Forks.

Livy then claims immediate revenge, but modern historians, following hints in Cicero and Appian and Rome's activity elsewhere, generally believe that the Caudine peace held until 316: Rome lost Fregellae and Cales, while building alliances in Apulia (Teanum Apulum and Canusium in 318), sending prefects to Capua and creating new tribes. When war resumed in 316-315, Rome took Saticula but suffered a defeat at Lautulae that cut the coast road and caused revolts among the Aurunci, at Sora and in Capua. Rome recovered in 314, destroying the Ausonian towns, retaking Sora and founding a colony at Luceria, and in 313-312 took Nola and planted colonies at Suessa, Pontiae, Saticula and Interamna. In 312 Appius Claudius built the Via Appia. A second front opened with the Etruscan war of 311-308, but Rome took Bovianum (311), won the battle of the gilded shields (309) and Bovianum again (305), capturing the Samnite general Statius Gellius. In 304 the Samnites renewed the old treaty.

Salmon's study remains the best reconstruction; Livy's annual victories are inflated, and Diodorus sometimes records Roman defeats that Livy omits. The war's outcome was strategic: Samnium was encircled by colonies, alliances and roads, Campania secured, and northern Apulia brought into the Roman orbit, setting the stage for the decisive Third Samnite War.

In 311, as their forty-year truces with Rome expired, the Etruscan cities, all except Arretium according to Livy, besieged the Roman ally and colony of Sutrium, the 'gateway of Etruria' on the edge of the Ciminian forest. The consul Q. Aemilius Barbula fought an indecisive battle there. In 310 Q. Fabius Rullianus, consul for the second time, sent his brother, who spoke Etruscan, disguised as a herdsman through the dense Ciminian forest, which no Roman had crossed, and then led his army through it into the rich lands of central Etruria. The Senate, alarmed, sent envoys to forbid the venture, but they arrived too late. Fabius ravaged the country, won battles near Perusia and Sutrium, and made the Umbrian Camertes allies on equal terms. Perusia, Cortona and Arretium obtained thirty-year truces.

Livy places a hard-fought victory at Lake Vadimon in 310 against an Etruscan army bound by a sacred law, perhaps the same as Diodorus' battle near Perusia. In 308 Fabius defeated the Umbrians at Mevania, Tarquinii obtained a forty-year truce, and several towns of Volsinii were stormed. Diodorus independently records Fabius' victories in Umbria and Etruria, which supports the tradition despite its Fabian colouring.

The war revealed the weakness of the Etruscan cities: unable to coordinate, each made separate terms. Rome now dealt with individual Etruscan states, in 302 intervening at Arretium to restore the aristocratic Cilnii against their commons, a pattern repeated at Volsinii in 265. The crossing of the Ciminian forest became a symbol of Roman boldness, and Livy uses it to describe the forest as more trackless than the German forests of his own day. The war also forced Rome to fight on two fronts while the Samnite war continued, a test it passed.

In 298 the Lucanians, attacked by the Samnites, sought Roman alliance, and Rome declared war. L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus campaigned in Samnium and Lucania, as his elogium claims (Livy sends him to Etruria), and Bovianum and Aufidena were taken. In 297 Q. Fabius Rullianus and P. Decius Mus won at Tifernum and Maleventum. In 296 the Samnite general Gellius Egnatius led an army north to Etruria to build a coalition with the Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls, while Samnite raiders swept Campania until L. Volumnius caught them on the Volturnus; Rome founded citizen colonies at Minturnae and Sinuessa.

The crisis of 295 began with the destruction of a Roman legion near Camerinum by the Gauls. Both consuls marched north and, at Sentinum, Fabius and Decius defeated the Samnites and Gauls while a diversion kept the Etruscans and Umbrians at home; Decius devoted himself, and Gellius Egnatius fell. In 294 M. Atilius Regulus fought near Luceria, L. Postumius Megellus took Rusellae, and Volsinii, Perusia and Arretium obtained truces for 500,000 asses each. In 293 the Samnites raised a 'linen legion' of 16,000 nobles sworn by a terrible oath to fight to the death, but L. Papirius Cursor destroyed their army at Aquilonia while Sp. Carvilius took Cominium. Papirius paid into the treasury 2,533,000 asses of heavy bronze, raised largely from the sale of captives, and 1,830 pounds of silver; Carvilius cast a colossal Jupiter from Samnite armour. In 292 Q. Fabius Gurges, after a defeat, captured Gavius Pontius, who was executed in 291, and a huge Latin colony was sent to Venusia. In 290 M'. Curius Dentatus forced the Samnites to make peace and conquered the Sabines and Praetuttii.

The war decided the fate of Italy. The anti-Roman coalition was broken, Samnite power reduced, and Roman territory extended across the peninsula to the Adriatic. The plague of 293-292, which brought Aesculapius to Rome, and the debt crisis that led to the lex Hortensia in 287, show the cost.

Polybius gives the essential account. Ten years after Sentinum the Gauls besieged Arretium; the Romans marched to its relief and were defeated before the city, the commander, L. Caecilius Metellus, being killed. His successor M'. Curius sent envoys to negotiate the return of prisoners, but the Senones murdered them. The Romans at once invaded the territory of the Senones, killed most of them, expelled the rest and planted the colony of Sena Gallica (Senigallia) on the coast, the first Roman colony on the Adriatic. The Boii, fearing the same fate, joined the Etruscans and marched on Rome but were crushed at Lake Vadimon (283); the next year they tried again, were defeated once more (Livy's Periochae and later writers place a battle near Populonia), and made a peace that held for 45 years.

Livy's version, preserved only in summary and in later writers, credits the consul P. Cornelius Dolabella (283) with the destruction of the Senones and the victory at Vadimon, and Appian adds that the Senonian chief Britomaris killed the Roman envoys to avenge his father, killed at Arretium. The chronology of the three campaigns and the attribution of commands are tangled, but the outcome is clear.

The annexation of the ager Gallicus, the coastal strip from the Aesis to the Utens south of Ariminum, was the first conquest of Gallic land by Rome. It brought Roman territory to the edge of the Po valley; the Latin colony at Ariminum (268) followed. When the tribune C. Flaminius had the ager Gallicus distributed in individual allotments to Roman citizens in 232, Polybius says, the Boii and Insubres saw it as a threat to their own existence, and the great Gallic war of 225-222 began. The war of 284-282 thus opened the conflict that ended with the Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul.

The war began when Tarentum attacked a Roman squadron in its gulf and expelled the Roman garrison from Thurii in 282, then humiliated Rome's envoy. After the consul L. Aemilius Barbula ravaged its territory in 281, Tarentum invited Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, the most celebrated general of the Hellenistic world. He landed in 280 with some 25,000 men and 20 elephants, and defeated the consul P. Valerius Laevinus at Heraclea. The Lucanians, Samnites, Bruttii and several Greek cities joined him, and the Campanian garrison seized Rhegium. Pyrrhus marched north to within about 60 km of Rome, but the Latin allies held firm and the Senate, roused by the blind Appius Claudius, refused Cineas' peace proposals while the king stood in Italy. Fabricius negotiated the prisoners' release.

In 279 Pyrrhus won again at Ausculum, at heavy cost. Rome renewed its alliance with Carthage, whose admiral Mago brought 120 ships to Ostia. In 278 Fabricius returned the king's would-be poisoner, and Pyrrhus accepted the call of the Sicilian Greeks against Carthage. In Sicily he took Eryx, Panormus and almost all the Punic province except Lilybaeum, but his autocratic rule alienated the Sicilians. Meanwhile the Romans recovered ground in the south: Rufinus took Croton, Locri returned to Rome, though the Samnites defeated a consular army in the Cranita hills. In 276 Pyrrhus came back to Italy, losing ships in the Strait and plundering Locri; in 275 M'. Curius checked him near Maleventum, and he returned to Greece. His garrison in Tarentum surrendered in 272, the year of his death at Argos, and the Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttii submitted.

The war established Rome as a Mediterranean power. Ptolemy II sent an embassy of friendship in 273; colonies at Paestum, Cosa, Beneventum and Ariminum consolidated the gains; and the Carthaginian fleet's appearance at Tarentum in 272 foreshadowed the next conflict. Above all, Rome had shown that its system of alliances and inexhaustible manpower could defeat a Hellenistic army, a lesson Polybius and later Greek observers took seriously.

The Picentes, Sabellian inhabitants of the central Adriatic coast between the Aesis and the Aternus, had made a treaty with Rome in 299. Their culture is known from rich warrior graves and from the South Picene inscriptions, among the oldest Sabellian texts. In 269 they revolted, perhaps provoked by the Roman colonies in the ager Gallicus to their north and the loss of the Praetuttian land to their south. In 268 the consuls P. Sempronius Sophus and Ap. Claudius Russus fought them in a battle during which an earthquake struck; Sophus vowed a temple to Tellus, the Earth, which was built on the site of the razed house of Sp. Cassius. Both consuls triumphed.

Pliny says that 360,000 Picentes came into Rome's power, a figure that may refer to the whole population. Part of them were deported to the coast of the Gulf of Salerno around Picentia, the ager Picentinus; Asculum remained an ally; and Latin colonies were founded at Ariminum (268), on the border of Umbria and the former Senonian land, and at Firmum (264). In the same years the Sabines received full citizenship (268), the Umbrian Sarsinates were subdued (266), and the Sallentini of the heel of Italy were conquered, with the port of Brundisium (267-266).

The Picene war completed Roman control of the Adriatic coast from Ariminum to Apulia. The Picentes remained loyal through the Second Punic War, but Picenum was where the Social War began in 91, when the people of Asculum massacred Roman citizens, and later the region was the power base of Pompeius Strabo and his son Pompey, whose family estates and clientelae lay there.

Volsinii (Etruscan Velzna, modern Orvieto) was one of the richest Etruscan cities and the site of the federal sanctuary of Voltumna. It had fought Rome in 392-391, 308, 294 and 280. According to the later sources (Zonaras abridging Dio, Valerius Maximus, Orosius and Florus), the Volsinian aristocracy had gradually handed military and political functions to their dependents, described as slaves or freedmen, who took over the government, married the nobles' widows and daughters, controlled wills and excluded the old families. In 265 the nobles secretly appealed to Rome. The consul Q. Fabius Gurges besieged the city and was mortally wounded; in 264 the consul M. Fulvius Flaccus starved Volsinii into surrender, executed the rebels, restored the nobles, razed the city and resettled the survivors on a new site by Lake Bolsena, Volsinii Novi.

Fulvius triumphed on 1 November 264. Metrodorus of Scepsis, quoted by Pliny, said Rome took Volsinii for the sake of its 2,000 statues. Fulvius brought the city's god Vortumnus to Rome, probably by evocatio, and dedicated a temple to him on the Aventine; an inscribed base found at Sant'Omobono in the Forum Boarium records his dedication 'Volsinio capto'. The Fanum Voltumnae, the meeting place of the Etruscan league, lost its political role.

Modern historians interpret the 'slaves' as Etruscan dependents (perhaps the lautni, a class of freedmen or serfs attested in inscriptions), or as lower-class citizens enfranchised by the aristocracy in times of war, rather than chattel slaves. Rome's intervention to restore an aristocracy, as at Arretium in 302, shows the social basis of Roman hegemony in Italy: alliance with local elites. The war ended Etruscan independence in the same year in which Rome voted to aid the Mamertines and crossed into Sicily.
